explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. One of His disciples says, "Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples" (Luke 11:1). He doesn't ask for a miracle or a fancy speech. He asks about prayer, and I love that he just said it out loud.

Healing is a big thing, friend, but it's not what this disciple asks for. Luke 11:1 says he requested, "Lord, teach us to pray." Jesus had just finished praying, and prayer is what the disciple brings up. I'd have forgotten my own question halfway through, so I'm impressed.
Fasting is a good guess, but this disciple doesn't ask about it. In Luke 11:1 he says, "Lord, teach us to pray." Nobody in this scene is skipping a meal yet. We'll get to bread soon enough, baker.

Yes, baker. The disciple says, "just as John taught his disciples" (Luke 11:1). He points at another teacher's students and says, in so many words, "Can we get some of that?" I respect a man who asks for what he wants.
Elijah is a name people know, but this disciple doesn't use it. Luke 11:1 says, "just as John taught his disciples." John is the teacher he names. Elijah can sit this one out.

Samuel's a fine name, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. The disciple asks Jesus to teach them "just as John taught his disciples" (Luke 11:1). The name he says is John. I'll keep Samuel on the bench for a different passage.

I see why you'd go there, friend, because a kingdom does come up in this prayer. But look at the very first word out of Jesus' mouth: "Father, hallowed be Your name" (Luke 11:2). What they call God first is Father. King isn't in that opening line, so this one is false.

That's right. Jesus says, "When you pray, say: 'Father, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come'" (Luke 11:2). The kingdom is in the prayer, but the first thing they call God is Father. That's the first word, baker, and it's a close one.

You got it, baker. Jesus says, "Give us each day our daily bread" (Luke 11:3). It's one day's bread at a time, like a batch that never has to last till next Tuesday. Honestly, that's my kind of schedule.

A whole week's worth sounds nice and tidy, friend. But Luke 11:3 says, "Give us each day our daily bread." The word is day, not week. Seven days of bread in one ask would be a lot of bread to carry anyway.

A year of bread in one go? That's a big order, baker. The prayer in Luke 11:3 asks, "Give us each day our daily bread." It's a day-sized request. You'd need one very large pantry for the year version.

Yes, baker. The prayer says, "for we also forgive everyone who sins against us" (Luke 11:4). The people asking God for forgiveness also say they forgive others. Forgiving is lighter to carry than a grudge, and I can tell you that from experience.

Warning people has its place, friend, but that's not what the prayer says. Luke 11:4 reads, "for we also forgive everyone who sins against us." The word is forgive. Nobody in this prayer is handing out warning labels.

Dodging someone in the hallway is a real thing people do, baker. But the prayer doesn't go that way. It says, "for we also forgive everyone who sins against us" (Luke 11:4). Forgive is the word Jesus gives them.
That's the one, baker. The prayer closes with, "And lead us not into temptation" (Luke 11:4). That's the last request Jesus gives them. It's short, and it's the finish.

Riches would be a nice add-on, friend, but they aren't in this prayer. It ends with, "And lead us not into temptation" (Luke 11:4). The last request is about temptation. I checked the whole prayer and found no wish list for treasure.
Enemies don't come up in the prayer, baker. Jesus ends it with, "And lead us not into temptation" (Luke 11:4). The last thing they ask for is about temptation. You can put the enemies down, friend.

Right on, baker. The man says, "because a friend of mine has come to me on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him" (Luke 11:6). A friend showed up from a trip, and the man had nothing to put in front of him. I'd have hidden in the pantry, honestly.

It's actually true, friend, and the story says so. The man tells his friend, "because a friend of mine has come to me on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him" (Luke 11:6). That's his reason for knocking. One guest, one journey, and an empty table.
That's what he says, baker. The friend inside answers, "Do not bother me" (Luke 11:7). It's not the warmest welcome at midnight, but it is a very honest one.

What a nice neighbor that would be, friend, but that's not what he says. The friend inside answers, "Do not bother me" (Luke 11:7). He doesn't open the door, let alone say come in. That's a different story from the one Jesus tells.

Sending him down the street is a clever move, baker, but the man inside doesn't say that. His first words are, "Do not bother me" (Luke 11:7). He doesn't point to any other house. He just wants to stay put.

That makes sense as a guess, friend, but the man never says it. What he says is, "Do not bother me. My door is already shut, and my children and I are in bed. I cannot get up to give you anything" (Luke 11:7). He talks about the shut door and being in bed, and he says nothing about the bread running out. So this one is false.

You've got it, baker. The man inside says, "My door is already shut, and my children and I are in bed. I cannot get up to give you anything" (Luke 11:7). The door and the bed are his reasons, and he never says he's out of bread. Good catch on what the text leaves out.

Bingo, baker. Jesus says that even though he will not get up "because of his friendship, yet because of the man's persistence, he will get up" (Luke 11:8). The man keeps asking, and that's what moves him. I know a few snooze buttons that could learn from this.

Money talks, friend, but it never gets a word in this story. Jesus says, "because of the man's persistence, he will get up" (Luke 11:8). Nobody offers a payment anywhere in the passage. The persistence does the work.

Neighbors peeking through their curtains is a fun picture, baker, but they're not in the story. Jesus says, "because of the man's persistence, he will get up" (Luke 11:8). The man's persistence is the reason, and the neighbors never come up.
That's what it says, baker. Luke 11:8 says he "will get up and give him as much as he needs." The man asked for three loaves, and the friend gives what he needs. Not a crumb short.

One loaf would be a stingy ending, friend, and that's not how Jesus tells it. Luke 11:8 says the friend "will get up and give him as much as he needs." He gives what the man needs, not a single loaf and a shrug.
Half sounds like a bargain bin, baker, but that's not in the story. Luke 11:8 says the friend "will get up and give him as much as he needs." The man gets what he needs, with nothing cut in half.
That's the word, baker. Jesus says, "knock, and the door will be opened to you" (Luke 11:9). It matches the midnight story, where a man stood knocking at a door. Ask, seek, knock. Easy to remember.
Tapping on a window at midnight would get some strange looks, friend. Jesus says, "knock, and the door will be opened to you" (Luke 11:9). It's a door, just like in the story He just told.

That one sounds big and holy, baker, but it's not the word here. Jesus says, "knock, and the door will be opened to you" (Luke 11:9). The knocking opens a door, the same kind the man in the story was standing at.
That's the one, baker. Jesus says, "For everyone who asks receives" (Luke 11:10). Everyone is a very big word, and it's the one He chose. I like a promise with no fine print.

That would shrink the line a lot, friend, but Jesus doesn't say it. He says, "For everyone who asks receives" (Luke 11:10). The word is everyone, with no list of who qualifies. That's good news for a stamper who spent years in a drawer.
Jesus is talking to His disciples here, baker, but listen to what He says. "For everyone who asks receives" (Luke 11:10). The word is everyone, and it doesn't stop at the people in the room.

I get why it sounds that way, friend, but look at how Jesus puts it. He asks, "What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead?" (Luke 11:11). He asks it as a question about what a father would do, and He follows with the egg and the scorpion (Luke 11:12). He's not saying many fathers hand over harmful things, so this one is false.

That's right, baker. Jesus asks, "What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead? Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion?" (Luke 11:11-12). He asks these as questions, and He doesn't say fathers do it. A snake for a fish would be a rough dinner.

That's what He says, baker. Jesus tells them, "if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children" (Luke 11:13). He says it plainly, and He doesn't dress it up. I'd have winced, but it sets up the best part right after.

It feels like a harsh thing to say, friend, but it's in the verse. Jesus says, "if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children" (Luke 11:13). He's honest about His listeners, and then He turns to what the Father does. So this one is true.

That's it, baker. Jesus says, "how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!" (Luke 11:13). The words "how much more" are right there. If fathers can give good gifts, the Father in heaven gives more.

It's not just a tie, friend. Jesus says, "how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!" (Luke 11:13). "How much more" tells us the Father goes further than the fathers in the story.

That's not how Jesus says it, baker. He says, "how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!" (Luke 11:13). There's no "only sometimes" in the verse. It's "how much more."
You got it, baker. Jesus says, "how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!" (Luke 11:13). That's the gift He names at the end. Ask, and the Father gives.

Long life is a gift many would ask for, friend, but it's not the one Jesus names. Luke 11:13 says the Father in heaven will "give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!" That's the gift at the end of the passage.

Great riches would be a fun answer, baker, but they're not here. Jesus says the Father in heaven will "give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!" (Luke 11:13). The Holy Spirit is the gift He names. I'll stick with that over a pile of treasure.
